prompt: Experiment 2 differed from Experiment 1 in which of the following ways?

choices.text: A different quantity was measured in Experiment 2 in place of the pitch of the song
choices.rationale: Both experiments measured the pitch of the song.

choices.text: The habitat was open grassland in Experiment 1 and dense forest in Experiment 2
choices.rationale: Correct. The description of Experiment 2 says the procedure was repeated with only this condition changed.

choices.text: The recording equipment was varied in Experiment 2 but held constant in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: The recording equipment was kept the same in both experiments; only the habitat changed.

choices.text: The body mass of the species was held constant in Experiment 2 but varied in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: Both experiments tested the same set of values of body mass.

explanation: Experiment 2 repeated Experiment 1 living in dense forest; everything else, including the values of body mass and the quantity measured, stayed the same.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Researchers recorded the songs of male birds of six species living in open grassland and measured the average pitch of each species' song. Body mass was taken as the average for adult males of the species. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated living in dense forest, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which of the following hypotheses is best supported by the results of Experiment 1?

choices.text: Increasing time decreases voltage.
choices.rationale: Correct. Every increase in the independent variable produced a smaller measured value.

choices.text: Voltage is greatest at an intermediate time and lower at both higher and lower values.
choices.rationale: The results never reverse direction, so there is no intermediate maximum.

choices.text: Time has no effect on voltage.
choices.rationale: The measured values change clearly from trial to trial, so there is an effect.

choices.text: The lamp used determines voltage.
choices.rationale: The lamp used was held constant, so the experiment says nothing about its effect.

explanation: Reading the results in order of time, the voltage of the battery decreased, which supports: "Increasing time decreases voltage."

stimulus.title: Battery Voltage Over Time
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students connected a fresh AA battery to a small lamp and measured the battery's voltage with a voltmeter at regular intervals while the lamp stayed on.
Results (the voltage of the battery): at 0 h, 1.61 V; at 2 h, 1.54 V; at 4 h, 1.42 V; at 6 h, 1.27 V; at 8 h, 1.08 V.

prompt: Why did the experimenters most likely time 10 complete swings and divide by 10 rather than time a single swing in Experiment 1?

choices.text: Remove the need to keep the angle from which the bob was released the same
choices.rationale: Repetition does not substitute for controlling variables; controls are still needed.

choices.text: Increase the range of string length that could be tested
choices.rationale: Repeating a measurement does not change which values of string length are tested.

choices.text: Make the period of the pendulum change more in response to string length
choices.rationale: Repeating a measurement cannot change the size of the real effect.

choices.text: Reduce the effect of random error in individual measurements
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging repeated measurements cancels out much of the random variation in any single measurement.

explanation: Any single measurement contains random error; repeating and averaging makes the recorded value more reliable.

stimulus.title: Pendulum Period
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students hung a metal bob from a string, pulled the bob 10° to one side, and released it. They timed 10 complete swings with a stopwatch and divided by 10 to find the period. The procedure was repeated for several string lengths.
Results (the period of the pendulum): at 20 cm, 0.88 s; at 40 cm, 1.25 s; at 60 cm, 1.53 s; at 80 cm, 1.77 s; at 100 cm, 1.97 s; at 120 cm, 2.16 s.

prompt: Suppose the experimenters had run one more trial in Experiment 1 at a time of 1 h. Based on the results, the voltage of the battery in that trial would most likely have been:

choices.text: between 1.55 V and 1.61 V
choices.rationale: Correct. 1 h is between the tested values 0 h and 2 h, whose results were 1.55 and 1.61.

choices.text: above every result obtained, greater than 1.61 V
choices.rationale: This is above every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

choices.text: below every result obtained, less than 1.07 V
choices.rationale: This is below every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

choices.text: between 1.47 V and 1.55 V
choices.rationale: This interval belongs to time between 2 h and 4 h.

explanation: The results change steadily with time, so a trial at 1 h should give a value between those of its neighbors, 1.55 and 1.61 V.

stimulus.title: Battery Voltage Over Time
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students connected a fresh AA battery to a small lamp and measured the battery's voltage with a voltmeter at regular intervals while the lamp stayed on.
Results (the voltage of the battery): at 0 h, 1.61 V; at 2 h, 1.55 V; at 4 h, 1.47 V; at 6 h, 1.36 V; at 8 h, 1.23 V; at 10 h, 1.07 V.

prompt: Why did the experimenters most likely measure the tread depth at 5 values of distance driven spread across a range, instead of at only the lowest and highest values?

choices.text: Remove the need to hold the car used constant during the trials
choices.rationale: Testing more values does not replace controlling other variables.

choices.text: Make each individual measurement of the tread depth more precise than it would otherwise be
choices.rationale: The precision of a single measurement depends on the instrument and repetition, not on how many values of the independent variable are tested.

choices.text: Show how the tread depth changes across the whole range, not just at its two ends
choices.rationale: Correct. Two points can only show a difference; several points show the shape of the relationship.

choices.text: Keep the tread depth the same from one trial to the next so that the trials could be compared
choices.rationale: The dependent variable is measured, not held constant; it is expected to change.

explanation: Measuring at several values of distance driven lets the experimenters see the pattern of the relationship, not just whether the two ends differ.

stimulus.title: Distance Driven and Tire Wear
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
A testing company fitted new tires of one model to the same car and measured the tread depth with a gauge after each 10,000 km of driving on a fixed route.
Results (the tread depth): at 0 km, 8.9 mm; at 10000 km, 7.9 mm; at 20000 km, 6.8 mm; at 30000 km, 5.8 mm; at 40000 km, 4.7 mm.

prompt: If the experimenters wanted their measurements of the horizontal distance the ball traveled to be more reliable, they should most likely:

choices.text: Allow the compression of the spring to vary freely from one trial to the next
choices.rationale: Letting a controlled variable vary adds a confounding factor and makes results less reliable.

choices.text: Repeat each trial several more times at each launch angle and average the results
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging more repeated trials reduces the effect of random error.

choices.text: Test fewer values of launch angle so that each individual trial can be done more quickly
choices.rationale: Fewer values give less information and do nothing to reduce random error.

choices.text: Record the horizontal distance the ball traveled to fewer decimal places to simplify the table
choices.rationale: Rounding discards information; it cannot make the results more trustworthy.

explanation: Reliability improves when random variation is averaged out by more repetitions or larger samples, while everything else is held constant.

stimulus.title: Launch Angle and Range
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students used a spring launcher to fire the same ball at a set angle above the horizontal, always with the spring compressed by the same amount. They measured the horizontal distance from the launcher to the landing point. Each angle was fired three times and the average distance recorded.
Results (the horizontal distance the ball traveled): at 20°, 14.4 m; at 30°, 18.7 m; at 40°, 20.5 m; at 50°, 19.9 m; at 60°, 17.0 m; at 70°, 12.3 m.

prompt: Which of the following best describes how the procedure of Experiment 2 differed from that of Experiment 1?

choices.text: The thickness of the insulation was held constant in Experiment 2 but varied in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: Both experiments tested the same set of values of insulation thickness.

choices.text: The inside temperature was 60°C inside in Experiment 1 and 80°C inside in Experiment 2
choices.rationale: Correct. The description of Experiment 2 says the procedure was repeated with only this condition changed.

choices.text: A different quantity was measured in Experiment 2 in place of the rate of heat loss
choices.rationale: Both experiments measured the rate of heat loss.

choices.text: The room temperature was varied in Experiment 2 but held constant in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: The room temperature was kept the same in both experiments; only the inside temperature changed.

explanation: Experiment 2 repeated Experiment 1 at 80°C; everything else, including the values of insulation thickness and the quantity measured, stayed the same.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students wrapped a metal box containing an electric heater in foam sheets of a set total thickness. They adjusted the heater power until the inside temperature held steady at 60°C in a 20°C room and recorded that power as the rate of heat loss. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated at 80°C, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which of the following hypotheses is best supported by the results of Experiment 1?

choices.text: Speed has no effect on stopping distance.
choices.rationale: The measured values change clearly from trial to trial, so there is an effect.

choices.text: Increasing speed increases stopping distance.
choices.rationale: Correct. Every increase in the independent variable produced a larger measured value.

choices.text: Increasing speed decreases stopping distance.
choices.rationale: The results do not fall with every increase in the independent variable.

choices.text: The car and its tires determines stopping distance.
choices.rationale: The car and its tires was held constant, so the experiment says nothing about its effect.

explanation: Reading the results in order of speed, the stopping distance increased, which supports: "Increasing speed increases stopping distance."

stimulus.title: Speed and Stopping Distance
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
On a closed test track, a driver brought the same car to each test speed, then braked as hard as possible when a signal light flashed. The distance from the signal to the stopping point was measured. Each speed was tested three times and the average distance recorded.
Results (the stopping distance): at 20 km/h, 7.8 m; at 40 km/h, 21.1 m; at 60 km/h, 40.1 m; at 80 km/h, 64.6 m; at 100 km/h, 94.8 m; at 120 km/h, 130.5 m.

Experiment 1

prompt: If Experiment 1 were extended with a trial at 17.5°, the mass of soil eroded would most likely have been:

choices.text: between 160 g and 244 g
choices.rationale: Correct. 17.5° is between the tested values 15° and 20°, whose results were 160 and 244.

choices.text: above every result obtained, greater than 342 g
choices.rationale: This is above every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

choices.text: below every result obtained, less than 38 g
choices.rationale: This is below every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

choices.text: between 244 g and 342 g
choices.rationale: This interval belongs to slope angle between 20° and 25°.

explanation: The results change steadily with slope angle, so a trial at 17.5° should give a value between those of its neighbors, 160 and 244 g.

stimulus.title: Slope and Soil Erosion
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students filled identical trays with 5 kg of the same soil, tilted each tray to a set angle, and sprinkled water evenly over it from a watering can. They collected the soil that washed out of the tray, dried it, and found its mass.
Results (the mass of soil eroded): at 5°, 38 g; at 10°, 92 g; at 15°, 160 g; at 20°, 244 g; at 25°, 342 g.

prompt: The experimenters tested 5 different values of the soaking time rather than just two. The most likely reason was to:

choices.text: Keep the percent of seeds that sprouted the same from one trial to the next so that the trials could be compared
choices.rationale: The dependent variable is measured, not held constant; it is expected to change.

choices.text: Remove the need to hold the number of seeds in each batch constant during the trials
choices.rationale: Testing more values does not replace controlling other variables.

choices.text: Make each individual measurement of the percent of seeds that sprouted more precise than it would otherwise be
choices.rationale: The precision of a single measurement depends on the instrument and repetition, not on how many values of the independent variable are tested.

choices.text: Show how the percent of seeds that sprouted changes across the whole range, not just at its two ends
choices.rationale: Correct. Two points can only show a difference; several points show the shape of the relationship.

explanation: Measuring at several values of soaking time lets the experimenters see the pattern of the relationship, not just whether the two ends differ.

stimulus.title: Seed Soaking and Germination
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students soaked batches of 50 radish seeds in water for a set number of hours, then placed each batch on damp paper towels in a covered tray. After 5 days they counted the seeds that had sprouted and converted the count to a percent.
Results (the percent of seeds that sprouted): at 4 h, 28%; at 8 h, 41%; at 12 h, 55%; at 16 h, 58%; at 20 h, 49%.

prompt: If the experimenters wanted their measurements of the sound intensity to be more reliable, they should most likely:

choices.text: Repeat each trial several more times at each distance and average the results
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging more repeated trials reduces the effect of random error.

choices.text: Allow the height of the sound meter to vary freely from one trial to the next
choices.rationale: Letting a controlled variable vary adds a confounding factor and makes results less reliable.

choices.text: Test fewer values of distance so that each individual trial can be done more quickly
choices.rationale: Fewer values give less information and do nothing to reduce random error.

choices.text: Record the sound intensity to fewer decimal places to simplify the table
choices.rationale: Rounding discards information; it cannot make the results more trustworthy.

explanation: Reliability improves when random variation is averaged out by more repetitions or larger samples, while everything else is held constant.

stimulus.title: Distance and Sound Intensity
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
In an open field, students placed a speaker playing a steady tone and used a sound meter to measure the intensity at several distances along a straight line from the speaker. Readings were taken at the same height above the ground.
Results (the sound intensity): at 1 m, 81.8 µW/m²; at 2 m, 20.4 µW/m²; at 3 m, 9.1 µW/m²; at 4 m, 5.1 µW/m²; at 5 m, 3.3 µW/m².
